_meta.note: Synthetic baseline derived from Tholonic N-D-C framework applied to intellectual history of economics. D and C values represent constraint and output magnitudes per epoch. N is emergent intellectual-institutional equilibrium.

synthetic.label: Synthetic Baseline
synthetic.description: Chain-average N-D-C values across all 10 epochs, pre-3000 BCE to present

2.name: Medieval Commercial Revolution
2.paradigm_state: Ledger credit and bill of exchange

0.balance_zone_note: High D from geographic isolation and oral tradition. Low C from limited exchange outputs. Strong imbalance reflects pre-literate constraint-heavy epoch.
0.notes: Gift and tribute economies. Temple redistribution. Weight-based commodity standards emerging. No written economic theory.
0.data_quality: Low: oral tradition only; primary sources are sparse clay tablet archives
0.opacity_reason: Oral transmission, undeciphered scripts, incomplete archaeological record
0.key_transition_trigger: Coinage adoption displaces barter commodity standards

1.balance_zone_note: Metal supply and war finance constraints (D) remain heavy. C begins growing as coinage and commercial law diffuse but social hierarchy limits adoption.
1.notes: Lydian coinage c. 600 BCE. Aristotle on exchange value. Roman commercial law formalizes contracts. Market price signals emerge.
1.data_quality: Low-Medium: surviving texts and coin hoards; Roman legal records more complete
1.opacity_reason: Language barriers, incomplete archives, Roman-era document destruction
1.key_transition_trigger: Roman collapse removes empire D; church and guild structures absorb C outputs

2.balance_zone_note: First coherent epoch. D remains high from usury prohibition and jurisdictional fragmentation but C outputs (bill of exchange, double-entry) partially resolve D constraints through legal fictions.
2.notes: Bill of exchange circumvents usury. Medici Bank (1397). Champagne fair networks. Pacioli Summa (1494). Deposit banking in Italian city-states.
2.data_quality: Medium: merchant account books survive; guild records; partial archives in Italian cities
2.opacity_reason: Private merchant records; political destruction of archives; language diversity
2.key_transition_trigger: Printing press enables mercantilist text diffusion; state consolidation creates new D

3.balance_zone_note: D and C more balanced as state institutions regularize trade. Bullionist D is coherent with colonial C. National debt instruments provide a new C channel that partially relaxes bullion D.
3.notes: VOC (1602). Bank of England (1694). Navigation Acts. Balance-of-trade statistics begin. Mercantilist treatises published.
3.data_quality: Medium: state records available; colonial archives partial; corporate records (VOC) good
3.opacity_reason: Colonial extraction records politically suppressed; private trading company accounts
3.key_transition_trigger: Industrial Revolution invalidates bullionist doctrine; Smith demolishes mercantilist D analytically

4.balance_zone_note: C slightly exceeds D as industrial outputs outpace theoretical constraints. Near-optimal balance. Paradigm is highly productive. First epoch where C > D.
4.notes: Wealth of Nations (1776). Ricardo comparative advantage (1817). Mill Principles (1848). Political economy chairs established. Economic journals founded.
4.data_quality: High: major published works; early statistical tables; trade data in public records
4.opacity_reason: Factory-level data private; colonial labor cost data suppressed
4.key_transition_trigger: Mathematical formalization makes labor value theory untenable; marginal analysis displaces classical D

5.balance_zone_note: C exceeds D as mathematical methods proliferate faster than disciplinary constraints. Highly productive period. Sustainability drops because C-D gap widens.
5.notes: Jevons (1871). Walras general equilibrium (1874). Marshall Principles (1890). PhD programs. Pareto optimum. Welfare economics.
5.data_quality: High: published mathematical proofs, peer-reviewed journals, statistical tables
5.opacity_reason: Firm-level cost data private; monopoly behavior under-reported
5.key_transition_trigger: Great Depression 1929: equilibrium model cannot explain persistent unemployment. N collapses.

6.balance_zone_note: Highest N in the chain. D and C nearly balanced (best sustainability). Crisis pressure converts into institutional innovation: every D constraint generates a corresponding C response. Most productive epoch.
6.notes: General Theory (1936). National income accounting (Kuznets). Bretton Woods (1944). IMF and World Bank. Welfare state. Development economics.
6.data_quality: High: detailed policy records; national accounts; IMF and World Bank data from 1944
6.opacity_reason: Cold War classified policy records; Soviet bloc data absent
6.key_transition_trigger: Stagflation 1973-79: simultaneous inflation and unemployment cannot be explained by IS-LM

7.balance_zone_note: Best sustainability score in chain due to near-perfect D-C balance. Stagflation crisis generates tight alignment between constraint diagnosis (D) and policy response (C). Volcker disinflation succeeds.
7.notes: Friedman monetarism. Lucas critique (1976). Volcker shock 1979-82. Rational expectations. Reagan-Thatcher supply-side. Central bank independence.
7.data_quality: High: central bank records, BLS, Federal Reserve historical data
7.opacity_reason: Political economy of deregulation: regulatory capture not fully documented
7.key_transition_trigger: Financialization and capital account liberalization generate new C beyond monetarist D framework

8.balance_zone_note: C significantly exceeds D as financial engineering proliferates faster than regulatory constraint. Balance still coherent but sustainability is low. Classic pre-crisis C overshoot pattern.
8.notes: Washington Consensus (1989). WTO (1995). DSGE models. CDO and CDS expansion. Global derivatives notional $683 trillion by 2007.
8.data_quality: High: BIS derivatives data, WTO trade statistics, IMF WEO; some OTC data opaque
8.opacity_reason: Over-the-counter derivatives unregistered; shadow banking off balance sheet; offshore flows
8.key_transition_trigger: Global Financial Crisis 2008: C overshoot resolves catastrophically. Efficient market D falsified.
8.custodian: IMF, World Bank, and economic policy institutes

9.balance_zone_note: Stressed epoch. D constraints weakened by model failure and political legitimacy crisis. C outputs proliferating but not converging. No child N has stabilized. Paradigm is open.
9.notes: GFC 2008. Piketty Capital (2014). Zero lower bound. MMT. Complexity economics. Behavioral mainstream. COVID-19 fiscal response. AI enters economics.
9.data_quality: Medium: ongoing; contested interpretations; pre-publication research visible but unverified
9.opacity_reason: Contested narratives; central bank balance sheet complexity; cryptocurrency and shadow finance
9.key_transition_trigger: Pending. Candidate N-states: climate macro, AI-augmented planning, degrowth steady-state, MMT-informed policy.
9.custodian: Distributed and contested: central banks, heterodox institutes, tech firms, governments

synthetic.interpretation: The intellectual supply chain of economics shows a clear developmental arc: stressed epochs in early history (oral tradition, sparse records) give way to coherent high-N epochs as institutional capacity and data quality improve. The Keynesian epoch (Phase 6) achieves the highest N and best sustainability through tight D-C balance under crisis pressure. The current post-2008 epoch is stressed, indicating a paradigm whose C outputs have outrun its D constraints and whose child N has not yet stabilized.
